HomeEssentials Inc. - Q4 FY2024 Earnings Call Transcript

Operator:
Good morning, everyone, and welcome to the HomeEssentials Inc. Q4 FY2024 Earnings Conference Call. All participants will be in listen-only mode. After today's presentation, there will be an opportunity to ask questions. [Operator Instructions] Please also note, today's event is being recorded.

I would now like to turn the conference over to Sarah Johnson, Head of Investor Relations. Please go ahead.

Sarah Johnson, Head of Investor Relations:
Thank you, Operator. Good morning, and thank you for joining us today to discuss HomeEssentials Inc.'s results for the Q4 FY2024. Joining me on today’s call are Mike Thompson, Chief Executive Officer; Lisa Chen, Chief Financial Officer; David Ruiz, Chief Merchandising Officer; and Emily Patel, Chief Stores Officer.

Before we begin, I would like to remind you that this call contains forward-looking statements, which are subject to risks and uncertainties. Please refer to our SEC filings for a complete discussion of these risks.

With that, I’ll turn the call over to Mike Thompson.

Mike Thompson, Chief Executive Officer:
Thank you, Sarah. Good morning, everyone. Thank you for joining us today. I’m pleased to report HomeEssentials Inc.'s performance for the Q4 FY2024. We continued to execute on our strategic priorities and delivered solid results despite the challenging macroeconomic environment.

Our overall performance reflected resilience, with total revenue growth and positive same-store sales amid consumer caution on discretionary spending. E-commerce growth accelerated through our omnichannel efforts, capturing more digital demand while leveraging store fulfillment. Store performance held steady, with traffic stabilizing in key regions thanks to targeted initiatives. Marketing initiatives proved effective, driving attributable sales lifts and higher returns on ad spend. Supply chain optimization kept inventory disciplined and reduced costs. Finally, our loyalty program update showed strong member engagement, boosting repeat visits and basket sizes.

We are confident in our ability to navigate the current environment and deliver long-term value for our shareholders.

Now, I'll turn the call over to Lisa Chen to provide more details on our financial results.

Lisa Chen, Chief Financial Officer:
Thank you, Mike. Good morning. I'll provide a more detailed review of our financial performance for the Q4 FY2024.

Our total revenue for the quarter was $2.90 billion, a 5.6% increase compared to the same period last year, driven by a 3.2% comp in same-store sales and contributions from new store openings and digital channels.

Gross margin came in at 36.0%, contracting 45 basis points year-over-year, primarily driven by persistent shrinkage pressures, elevated markdown activity, and some unfavorable mix shifts, partially offset by private label expansion and freight cost relief.

Let me dive deeper into one of the key headwinds we've been actively managing: shrinkage, with a particular focus on theft and its direct drag on gross margin. Shrinkage—or inventory shrink—remains a persistent challenge across the brick-and-mortar retail landscape, exacerbated by the surge in organized retail crime we've seen industry-wide since 2021. For context, the National Retail Federation's 2023 Shrink Survey pegged the U.S. average at 1.6% of sales, up from 1.3% pre-pandemic, and we're tracking right in line with that at our fiscal year-end shrink rate of 1.52% of net sales, a 25 basis point deterioration from 1.27% in FY23.

To quantify the impact: this elevated shrink level shaved approximately 38 basis points off our consolidated gross margin in Q4, contributing significantly to the year-over-year contraction. Breaking it down further, theft accounted for roughly 65% of total shrink, or about 0.99% of sales, with the remainder split between administrative errors (20%), vendor discrepancies (10%), and damage/spoilage (5%). High-velocity categories like consumer electronics—think AirPods, Dyson vacuums, and Nintendo Switch consoles—drove 40% of theft-related losses, followed by beauty and personal care at 25% (e.g., high-end skincare like La Mer and Charlotte Tilbury), and apparel/athleisure at 20%. These aren't isolated incidents; ORC rings are increasingly targeting smash-and-grab hits on these SKUs, mirroring patterns we've seen at peers like Ulta Beauty and Best Buy.

Regionally, the story varies significantly, underscoring the brick-and-mortar footprint's exposure. In our high-density urban markets—California, New York metro, and the Southeast—we saw shrink rates spike to 1.8-2.1% of sales, fueled by ORC hubs like the Bay Area and NYC boroughs. For instance, Proposition 47 in California continues to limit theft prosecutions under $950, enabling bolder operations, much like the challenges Target cited in their own earnings last quarter. Conversely, our Midwest and rural formats held steady at 1.1-1.3%, benefiting from lower foot traffic density and community-based loss prevention. Internationally, our 300 U.K. and Canadian stores fared better at 1.35%, thanks to stricter enforcement and CCTV saturation.

Trend-wise, Q4 marked the peak of a multi-quarter uptick: shrink rose from 1.35% in Q1 to 1.52% by year-end, aligning with NRF data showing a 20% YoY increase in ORC incidents. This isn't just anecdotal—our internal analytics, powered by our HomeEssentials Inventory Optimization Platform, flagged a 15% rise in 'empty shelf' scans in electronics bays and a 12% uptick in 'booster bag' detections at self-checkout lanes.

That said, we're not standing still. We've deployed over $150 million in FY24 capex toward shrink mitigation, targeting a 20-30 bps gross margin lift by FY26. Key technical initiatives include AI-driven computer vision: rolled out GenAI cameras from our partner Verkada across 2,500 high-risk stores, achieving 92% accuracy in real-time anomaly detection—like loitering or concealment. Early pilots reduced theft by 18% in deployed California supercenters. RFID expansion: tagging 70% of our beauty and electronics SKUs with Impinj RAIN RFID by Q2 FY25, up from 35% today. This mirrors Walmart's playbook and has already cut apparel scan-based trading variances by 22% in test markets. Self-checkout optimization: integrated NCR's AIGuard software with facial recognition and item-level intelligence, flagging 85% of fraudulent 'sweethearting' attempts. We've also capped self-checkout baskets at $100 in urban stores to deter ORC sweeps. Ecosystem partnerships: collaborating with the Retail Industry Leaders Association ORC task force and local PDs via our Secure Supply Chain initiative, sharing intel on 500+ repeat offenders. Plus, we're piloting 'spider wrap' and ink tags on Dyson and Sonos products, sourced from Checkpoint Systems.

Strategically, we're balancing deterrence with customer experience—avoiding overly aggressive gates that could alienate the 70% of our traffic that's omnichannel. Our Ship-from-Store BOPIS fulfillment now incorporates shrink-adjusted replenishment algorithms in our platform, shielding online margins from in-store losses. Looking forward, we expect FY25 shrink to moderate to 1.4% as these initiatives scale, adding 15-20 bps to gross margin expansion, net of $40 million in incremental opex. This positions us competitively against pure-plays like Amazon, where physical shrink is nil, while leveraging our 1,200-store network's scale. We're committed to transparency here—shrink is a margin killer, but our multi-layered approach gives us conviction in reversing the trend.

Turning to markdown activity and its effect on margins—a critical lever in our brick-and-mortar model where inventory productivity and pricing discipline are make-or-break in a promotional-heavy environment. In Q4, markdown activity totaled 12.8% of net sales, a meaningful improvement from 15.4% in the prior-year quarter and down sequentially from 13.9% in Q3. This represents our lowest markdown penetration in three years, reflecting the payoff from our proactive inventory management and the normalization of post-pandemic excess stock. For context, this is well below the S&P Retail Select Industry Index average of around 16-18% for apparel and home goods peers like Macy's or Kohl's, where aggressive clearance remains a drag amid softening consumer demand.

The margin impact contributed about 65 basis points to the compression. On a two-year stacked basis, however, margins expanded 180 bps, underscoring the structural progress we've made since the height of COVID-related inventory bloat.

Why the markdowns persisted? Seasonal headwinds: unseasonably warm weather in the Northeast and Midwest—our core 55% of store footprint—delayed outerwear and holiday prep sell-through by 10-15 days, necessitating promotional pricing on 25% of our fall assortment to hit 85%+ sell-through targets by quarter-end. In contrast, the Sun Belt regions (Southeast and Southwest, ~30% of sales) saw lighter markdowns at just 9.2% of sales, benefiting from stronger traffic in activewear and loungewear, up 4% comps there versus flat nationally. Competitive landscape: hyper-promoters like Walmart and Amazon continued to flood the market with deep discounts on private-label essentials—think their Great Value towels undercutting our margins by 15-20%—forcing us to match on high-velocity SKUs like fleece blankets and graphic tees. This was acute in home goods, where markdowns hit 18% of category sales versus 10% in apparel. Inventory dynamics: despite turns improving to 4.1x from 3.7x, we carried $150 million in excess fall/winter units from conservative spring buys, driving clearance sales that shaved average selling price by 7% to $42.50.

The good news—our technical initiatives are bending the curve. We've rolled out AI-powered dynamic markdown optimization across all 1,200 stores via our partnership with Blue Yonder, leveraging real-time RFID data from 95% of locations. This has improved markdown ROI by 22%, prioritizing store-level granularity: urban flagship stores in NYC and LA get fewer, targeted markdowns (under 10% of sales) on premium denim like our Madewell collabs, while suburban outlets see higher velocity clearances on basics. We've also piloted micro-fulfillment centers in 15 high-density markets, enabling BOPIS bundles that reduced markdown needs by 30% on promoted items by blending digital and physical inventory.

Strategically, we're laser-focused on margin-accretive growth. Private label now 42% of sales (up from 35%), with 45%+ gross margins versus 32% on branded goods—our 'HomeEssentials Peak Home' line cleared at just 8% markdown penetration, outpacing Macy's equivalents. We're tightening open-to-buy discipline with vendor scorecards, penalizing chronic over-deliveries, and accelerating off-price partnerships like our quarterly drops with Nordstrom Rack to offload aged inventory pre-markdown. Omnichannel is key too: ship-from-store on markdowned items boosted digital comps 12%, preserving store traffic without cannibalizing full-price sales.

Regionally, expect divergence: Northeast margins rebounding with winter normalization, targeting 39%+ in Q1 FY25; West Coast softness from California proposition impacts on casual apparel, where we'll lean into experiential store events to drive full-price traffic. Looking forward, we guide Q1 markdowns to 11-12% of sales, implying flat-to-up 20 bps gross margin sequentially, with FY2025 full-year at 38.2%. This assumes stable consumer sentiment—no recessionary pull-forward—and our $50 million inventory shrink target. Risks include further Temu/Shein deflation on fast fashion, but our loyalty program penetration at 68% (up 5 points) gives us pricing power on full-price tiers. We're proud of the progress—markdowns are no longer a margin black hole but a disciplined tool for inventory health.

Operating expenses were $679 million, representing 23.4% of revenue, with leverage from sales growth and productivity gains, though marketing investments weighed in.

Speaking of which, let's unpack our marketing and advertising expense trends, which continue to be a key lever in driving our omnichannel growth amid a softening brick-and-mortar traffic environment. Our total marketing and advertising spend came in at $178 million for the quarter, up 15% year-over-year from $155 million in Q4 2023. As a percentage of net sales, this represented 4.5%, a modest 20 basis point expansion from 4.3% last year, reflecting our disciplined approach to ROI optimization while accelerating customer acquisition and retention in a competitive landscape.

Breaking this down by category: digital marketing, which now accounts for 68% of our total spend—up from 52% a year ago—saw the sharpest increase at 28% YoY growth to $121 million. This shift is intentional and aligns with our 'Storefront Everywhere' strategy, where we're blurring the lines between physical stores and digital touchpoints. Key drivers include a 35% ramp-up in performance media on platforms like Google Ads, Meta, and TikTok, fueled by hyper-targeted campaigns around high-margin categories like kitchen appliances and sustainable home furnishings. For instance, our Google Performance Max campaigns delivered a 4.2x ROAS during Prime Day week, helping us capture share from pure-play e-tailers like Wayfair and Amazon Basics.

We've also doubled down on first-party data initiatives post the Chrome cookie deprecation, investing $12 million in our proprietary Customer Data Platform integrated with Snowflake for real-time personalization. This has powered AI-driven dynamic pricing promos and lookalike modeling, yielding a 22% uplift in conversion rates for our BOPIS program, which now represents 28% of digital orders. Social commerce is another bright spot—our shoppable Instagram Reels for outdoor patio collections generated $45 million in attributable sales at a blended CPA of just $18, outperforming industry benchmarks from peers like Target and Lowe's.

On the traditional side, comprising 25% of spend at $44 million, we saw a more muted 2% YoY increase as we optimize for efficiency. TV and connected TV remains our workhorse for brand awareness, with $28 million allocated to spots during peak events like the NBA Finals and summer grilling season. Print circulars and radio buys in our core Midwest markets—where we have over 450 superstores—held steady, supporting a 9% YoY traffic lift in those DMAs despite macroeconomic headwinds like persistent inflation in housing-related categories.

Regionally, our U.S. Sunbelt expansion is a standout: marketing dollars there grew 32% YoY to $52 million, focused on geo-fenced retargeting and partnerships with local influencers in high-growth MSAs like Phoenix and Atlanta. This drove a 14% comp store sales increase in those regions, outpacing the national average of 5.2%. In contrast, our Northeast footprint saw more tempered growth at 8% YoY, as we leaned into loyalty program enhancements for our HomeEssentials Rewards members—now 42 million strong—via personalized SMS and app push notifications, which boosted repeat visit rates by 16% without incremental ad spend.

Strategically, these trends underscore our pivot toward measurable, attributable growth in a brick-and-mortar world grappling with e-commerce encroachment and supply chain normalization. We're targeting a full-year FY25 marketing expense of $720-750 million, or 4.4-4.6% of sales, with digital expected to hit 72% of mix by year-end. This includes piloting AR/VR store tours in partnership with Snapchat for furniture visualization, which early tests show a 30% reduction in return rates, and expanding our affiliate program with creators in the #HomeRenovation space to rival IKEA's influencer playbook.

Looking ahead, we'll continue to stress-test every dollar through our marketing mix modeling, which incorporates econometric analysis of macroeconomic variables like consumer confidence and home price indices from the NAR. In Q1 FY25, expect heightened spend around back-to-school and holiday pre-planning, with a focus on driving traffic to our 1,200+ physical locations where 65% of sales still originate. This balanced approach not only supports our FY25 comp guidance of 4-6% but positions us for margin expansion as BOPIS efficiencies scale.

Our digital marketing effectiveness further highlights this strength. As we navigate a resilient but challenged brick-and-mortar retail landscape—marked by softening consumer discretionary spending amid 3.2% YoY inflation pressures and a 1.5% dip in U.S. foot traffic per Placer.ai data—our digital marketing engine remains a cornerstone of our omnichannel strategy. It delivered a standout 28% YoY increase in attributable store sales lift, contributing $247 million to our top line in Q4 alone. This isn't just about clicks or impressions; it's about precision-engineered campaigns driving incremental traffic to our 1,200 U.S. stores and 300 international locations, with a blended ROAS of 7.2x—up from 5.1x a year ago and ahead of peers like Target's reported 6.4x and Walmart's 6.8x.

Core metrics: ROAS hit 7.2x across $142 million in Q4 digital spend, a 41% improvement YoY, fueled by a 22% reduction in CAC to $18.47 per new high-value customer—defined as those spending $250+ L12M. Conversion rates from digital touchpoints to in-store purchases climbed to 4.8%, versus an industry benchmark of 3.2% per eMarketer, thanks to our proprietary closed-loop attribution model. This integrates first-party data from our Rewards loyalty program—42 million active members, up 15% YoY—with POS transaction data and geolocation signals. We're capturing 68% of our media lift through this, far surpassing the 45% average for multi-touch attribution in retail.

We've aggressively leaned into AI and machine learning to counter headwinds like Apple's ATT framework and Google's cookie phase-out. Our partnership with Adobe Experience Platform and Google Cloud's BigQuery has enabled a first-party data clean room, processing 2.5 petabytes of anonymized signals monthly. This powers hyper-personalized dynamic creative optimization, serving 1,200+ ad variants tailored to shopper intent—e.g., "weekend warrior" bundles for power tools during NFL season or "back-to-school refresh" kits for furniture. The result? A 31% uplift in CTRs to 2.14% on Google Performance Max campaigns, and a 47% boost in programmatic display ROAS to 8.1x via The Trade Desk's retail media integrations.

Geofencing remains a powerhouse for brick-and-mortar activation: we targeted 15-mile radii around high-traffic stores with "Store-in-a-Store" promotions, like our exclusive KitchenAid appliance pop-ups, driving a 12% lift in same-day visits per our MMM analysis. We've scaled CTV spend to 18% of our mix—up from 9% last year—leveraging Hulu and Roku for upper-funnel awareness. CTV attribution via pixel tracking showed a 5.9x ROAS and 2.3x higher basket sizes ($142 vs. $62 baseline).

Regionally, U.S. performance peaked at 7.8x ROAS, driven by robust iOS adoption and competitive pricing pressures pushing shoppers to physical showrooms. BOPIS orders surged 36% YoY to 2.1 million units, with digital ads attributing 62%—validating our $50 million investment in Shopify Plus headless integration. In Europe (210 stores across UK, Germany, France), ROAS moderated to 6.4x amid GDPR and high street footfall declines; we've pivoted to privacy-safe contextual targeting on Snapchat and TikTok. APAC (110 stores) delivered 8.9x ROAS, propelled by mobile penetration and WeChat Mini Programs—Douyin shoppable lives drove 1.4 million store visits.

Strategically, we're allocating 65% of our FY25 $650 million digital budget to lower-funnel tactics like our HomeEssentials Connect RMN, generating $28 million in Q4 ad revenue from CPG partners like P&G. We've embedded zero-party data via app quizzes, boosting LTV by 27%. Looking ahead, Q1 ROAS to 7.6x-8.0x, with holiday geofencing and AI bidding. In summary, digital marketing is our flywheel for resilience, delivering 3.2x ROI on incremental spend.

Moving to inventory levels, which remains a key pillar of our operational discipline. We ended Q4 FY2024 with total inventories of $1.28 billion, reflecting a disciplined 12% year-over-year decline from $1.45 billion in the prior-year period. This puts us roughly in line with our guidance midpoint and ahead of consensus. Active SKU count streamlined to 28,000 core SKUs across our 1,200 stores has helped focus on high-velocity items. Weeks of supply improved to 14.2 weeks from 16.8 weeks YoY, translating to an inventory turn rate of 4.1x for the quarter, up from 3.6x last year.

By segment: apparel (42% mix) declined 18% YoY to $540 million, post softer back-to-school; sell-through on fall arrivals hit 72% at full price, up 500 bps via Blue Yonder AI forecasting at 94% accuracy. Footwear/accessories down 5% to $320 million, buoyed by Nike/Crocs VMI covering 65% receipts. Home/hardlines (30%, $385 million) down 8% YoY but elevated sequentially for seasonal demand, with Sunbelt tailwinds.

Regionally, Midwest/Southeast at 12 WOS (-15% YoY); Northeast urban at 11 weeks (-20% YoY) via Manhattan Associates WMS upgrade, cutting shrinkage 22%. Initiatives: omnichannel sync reducing stockouts 35%; supplier forward commitments for fresher receipts (8% aged vs 14%); markdown engine liquidated $45 million, preserving 220 bps GM.

Forward, Q1 inventories to trough at $1.25 billion, targeting 10% further YoY cut by FY25 end, freeing $150 million working capital.

Net income was $310 million, or $0.82 per share. We generated $420 million in cash flow from operations. Inventory levels are currently $1.28 billion, down 12% YoY.

Now, turning to our outlook for Q1 FY2025 and full-year FY2025. Our guidance reflects cautious optimism grounded in the macro environment, consumer value-seeking, and our brick-and-mortar advantages enhanced by omnichannel.

For Q1, consolidated net sales $2.85 billion to $2.95 billion, 4% to 7% YoY growth, with SSS 2% to 4% (3-5% ex-53rd week). Hardlines/seasonal to lead mid-single digits, private label (28% sales) +500 bps GM uplift. Gross margin 35.8% to 36.3%, up 20-70 bps from mix, markdown discipline, freight down 15%. SG&A 23.5-24.0%, from Store Optimization Program (150 remodels, RFID shrink -25%). Adjusted op income $450-480 million, EPS $1.22-$1.32 (24.5% tax, 380M shares).

Sunbelt 5-7% SSS (new housing); Northeast/Midwest 0-2%. FY2025: sales $11.7-12.0B, 5-7% growth; SSS 3-5%; digital +12-15%. GM 36.0-36.5% (+100 bps private label 32%, ML markdowns -18% clearance). SG&A 23.0-23.5% ($150M savings, AI scheduling -20% OT). EBITDA $1.45-1.55B, EPS $5.10-5.40 (10-15% growth). Capex $450M (75 new stores, 200 remodels, micro-fulfillment).

Leaning into hybrid network (30% omnichannel FY26), sustainability (ENERGY STAR), loyalty personalization (+15% retention). Risks: tariffs, housing softness; mitigated by diversified sourcing.

We are maintaining a strong balance sheet and are well positioned to invest in our growth initiatives.

Now, I'd like to hand it over to David Ruiz, our Chief Merchandising Officer, to discuss our new product lines, and after that to Emily Patel to discuss store operations.

David Ruiz, Chief Merchandising Officer:
Thank you, Lisa. This quarter, we launched our sustainable smart home essentials line, which has seen strong uptake with 25% growth in the category and sell-through exceeding expectations by 15%. We are excited about the potential of this new product and other upcoming launches in private label appliances.

Emily Patel, Chief Stores Officer:
Thank you, David. We continue to focus on improving the customer experience in our stores. We have implemented AI-powered self-checkout kiosks and expanded RFID tagging in 80% of locations, resulting in faster transactions and a 12% reduction in wait times, with positive early feedback from customers.

Now, let's open the line for questions.

Operator:
Thank you. [Operator Instructions] Our first question comes from John Smith with Goldman Sachs. Please go ahead.

John Smith (Goldman Sachs):
Good morning. Can you provide more color on the impact of organized retail crime on your sales?

Mike Thompson, Chief Executive Officer:
Good morning, John. As Lisa outlined in detail, ORC drove much of our 1.52% shrink rate, accounting for 65% of losses and 38 basis points of gross margin pressure, particularly in urban markets and high-value SKUs like electronics and beauty. Our $150 million in mitigation tech, including Verkada AI cameras and RFID, is already showing 18% theft reductions in pilots, and we expect moderation to 1.4% next year.

Operator:
Our next question comes from Sarah Lee with Morgan Stanley. Please go ahead.

Sarah Lee (Morgan Stanley):
What are your expectations for same-store sales growth in the next quarter?

Lisa Chen, Chief Financial Officer:
Thanks, Sarah. For Q1 FY2025, we see SSS in the 2% to 4% range, accelerating modestly on holiday momentum, cooling inflation, and Sunbelt strength, with digital influencing more traffic.

Operator:
Our next question comes from Tom Wilson with Barclays. Please go ahead.

Tom Wilson (Barclays):
Can you elaborate on the supply chain improvements?

Mike Thompson, Chief Executive Officer:
Absolutely, Tom. Our optimizations include omnichannel inventory pooling cutting stockouts 35%, vendor early ship windows for fresher stock, and WMS upgrades reducing shrinkage 22% in key DCs. This drove 12% YoY inventory reduction while improving turns to 4.1x.

Operator:
Our next question comes from Lisa Grant with RBC Capital Markets. Please go ahead.

Lisa Grant (RBC Capital Markets):
What is the impact from the loyalty program?

Mike Thompson, Chief Executive Officer:
Great question, Lisa. With 42 million active members at 68% penetration, it's fueling 16% higher repeat rates via personalized offers, contributing to basket uplift and shielding full-price sales amid markdowns.

Operator:
Our next question comes from Mark Rivera with JPMorgan. Please go ahead.

Mark Rivera (JPMorgan):
Impressive details on digital marketing—can you expand on ROAS sustainability?

Lisa Chen, Chief Financial Officer:
Sure, Mark. Our 7.2x blended ROAS reflects first-party data clean rooms, AI DCO, and geofencing driving 4.8% conversions to store. We expect 7.6x-8.0x in Q1, with RMN revenue adding upside and buffers from high-margin influenced sales.

Operator:
There are no further questions at this time.

Mike Thompson, Chief Executive Officer:
Thank you for your questions. In closing, we are pleased with our progress this quarter and remain focused on executing our long-term strategy. Thank you for your continued support.

Sarah Johnson, Head of Investor Relations:
This concludes today's call. Thank you for joining us.
